106.title: Om gam ganapataye
106.howItsDone: Hindus commonly invoke Ganesha before beginning anything: a puja, a journey, a business, a wedding, an exam. Om Gam Ganapataye Namah is chanted in japa, often 108 times, especially on Wednesdays and on Ganesh Chaturthi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the panchakshara, Om Namah Shivaya: five syllables, bowing to Shiva. Your line was I bow to the stillness. Today, Shiva's son, and the mantra for starting things.

A new shop opens in Delhi, and before the first customer walks in, there's a small picture of Ganesha by the till with a garland on it. A student in Chennai writes a tiny Om or Ganesha's name at the top of an exam paper before the first answer. A wedding invitation opens with Ganesha on the front. A new car gets a little Ganesha on the dashboard. Whatever is starting, he's there first. You met him in the stories: the elephant head, the broken tusk, the race around his parents. Today, his mantra.
screen: `A NEW SHOP, A NEW EXAM.` → `A WEDDING, A NEW CAR.` → `GANESHA IS THERE FIRST.`

segments.voice: The mantra is Om Gam Ganapataye Namah. Take it apart. Om, the sound of everything. Gam, a single syllable called a bija, a seed: a sound that holds a whole deity inside it, the way a seed holds a tree. Gam is Ganesha's seed. The Ganapati Atharvashirsha, a hymn to Ganesha recited in homes and temples, describes how his sound is built, letter by letter. Ganapati means lord of the ganas, the hosts, the crowd of beings who follow Shiva, and the ending of Ganapataye means to. Then namah: I bow. So the whole thing is: Om, gam, to the lord of the hosts, I bow. Why is he the god of beginnings? One of his names is Vighneshvara, lord of obstacles. The stories say he removes them. And here's the surprise: some say he also places them, when a road shouldn't be taken yet. So people ask him first: clear the road, or show me where it's blocked. That's why Hindu rituals so often begin with a prayer to Ganesha before anything else, even a puja to another god. He's the doorway. It doesn't have to be something grand. A hard conversation is a beginning. So is a Monday, or opening your laptop. The mantra is a small pause at the door, asking that whatever's in the way be moved, or that you be shown the way around it. Clear the road.
screen: `GAM — GANESHA'S SEED SYLLABLE.` · `GANAPATI, LORD OF THE HOSTS.` · `LORD OF OBSTACLES, BOTH WAYS.` · `A PAUSE AT THE DOOR.` · then, large: `CLEAR THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind one thing you're about to begin, this week, tomorrow, even the next hour. Then, on beads or finger joints, do japa twenty-seven times: Om Gam Ganapataye Namah, slowly, letting the gam land softly, like something set down at a doorway. If you don't pray, let it be sound and counting, with the thing you're beginning in view, and at twenty-seven, rest.
Bija, a seed syllable that holds a deity inside it: gam, Ganesha's seed, in the mantra Om Gam Ganapataye, said before beginnings.
Your line: clear the road. Ganesha first, then everything else. Day one hundred six, done.

107.title: Hare Krishna
107.howItsDone: Gaudiya Vaishnavas, including members of ISKCON, chant the Hare Krishna maha-mantra daily on beads, often sixteen rounds of 108, and sing it together in kirtan with drums and cymbals, at home, in temples and in the street.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bija, Ganesha's seed in Om Gam Ganapataye, said at the door of beginnings. Your line was clear the road. Today, a mantra that's meant to be sung.

A group walks down a city street, in London or New York or Sydney, in saffron and white, with a drum and small hand cymbals, singing. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna. People stare, or smile, or cross the street. It can look like something new. It isn't. That same song filled the streets of a town in Bengal in the fifteen-hundreds, sung by a man who, his followers say, danced until he fell to the ground. And the words themselves are older still.
screen: `A DRUM AND CYMBALS DOWNTOWN.` → `IT LOOKS NEW. IT ISN'T.` → `A TOWN IN BENGAL, THE 1500S.`

segments.voice: Here are the words. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. Sixteen words, only three names. Krishna, the one you followed from the prison at midnight to the chariot. Rama, the prince who came home to a city of lamps. And Hare, which many devotees understand as calling on Hara, Radha, the love and energy of God, and which others hear as a form of Hari, Vishnu, the one who takes away. That's the maha-mantra, the great mantra. It appears, with the Rama half first, in a short text called the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, which says that in this age, the simplest way across is the name. Then, in the early fifteen-hundreds, in Navadvip in Bengal, came Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. His followers remember him as Krishna himself, come as a devotee, taking the names out of quiet rooms and into the street. Singing together, with drums and cymbals, is called sankirtan, and Chaitanya made it the heart of the practice. Why out loud? His tradition says the name isn't just a word about God; it carries God. Sung, it reaches everyone in earshot, even the ones crossing the street. In 1965, a monk in his line, an elderly man named A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami, arrived in New York with almost nothing. Before long he was singing it in a city park. That's where the group you saw comes from. The name, out loud.

segments.voice: This one isn't whispered: if you're somewhere you can, sing it softly, to any simple tune or on one note. Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. Once through is one round; keep going, and tap your knee for a drum if you like. If you don't pray, let it simply be singing, and notice what singing does that speaking doesn't; if you can't make noise, mouth the words.
Hare Krishna. The maha-mantra: sixteen words, three names, meant to be sung out loud.
Your line: the name, out loud. Some words are meant to be heard. See you tomorrow.

108.title: The Gayatri
108.howItsDone: Many Hindus chant the Gayatri at dawn and dusk as part of sandhya worship, often facing the sun and offering water; traditionally it is taught at the upanayana (sacred thread) ceremony, while many modern teachers and movements share it with all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hare Krishna, the great mantra, sung in the street. Your line was the name, out loud. Today, a verse from the Rig Veda, and it's about the sun.

Before dawn, on the steps down to the river at Varanasi, a man stands waist-deep in the water, facing east. He cups water in his hands, and as the first edge of the sun comes up, he lifts it, lets it pour back, and says a few lines under his breath. Far away in Delhi, a teenager hears the same lines on a phone, on the way to school. Same words, at the river and on the road, from a hymn far older than anyone saying them. It's called the Gayatri.
screen: `A MAN IN THE RIVER, FACING EAST.` → `THE SAME LINES ON A PHONE.` → `FAR OLDER THAN BOTH OF THEM.`

segments.voice: It comes from the Rig Veda, book three, hymn sixty-two, verse ten. Tradition says the sage Vishvamitra saw it. Gayatri is the name of its meter, three lines of eight syllables; the verse took the meter's name, and later came to be honored as a Goddess herself. Here it is, with the words traditionally said before it: Om bhur bhuvah svah, tat savitur varenyam, bhargo devasya dhimahi, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat. The first words name the three worlds: earth, the sky between, and heaven. Then it turns to Savitr, the sun, but not just the ball of fire: the sun as the one who stirs things into life and wakes everything up. We meditate on that radiance, the verse says. And the last line is the heart of it: may it stir, may it light up, our minds. Not give us things. Light, illuminate the mind. Something honest to know: traditions differ on who should chant it. Many hold that it's given at the sacred thread ceremony and chanted by the initiated, with care. Others, including many modern teachers and movements, have opened it to everyone. Both views are held by devout Hindus. So you don't have to say the Sanskrit at all. You can hold its meaning in English, which nobody restricts. The sun rises for everyone.

segments.voice: Sit facing a window if you can, or picture the sun just coming up. If your tradition welcomes you to chant it, say the last line softly, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat; if not, hold its meaning in English: light, illuminate the mind. Say it once, then hold it the way you'd hold your face toward the morning sun, and say it again when your attention drifts.
The Gayatri. A verse from the Rig Veda, to the sun who stirs everything awake, asking it to light up our minds.
Your line: light, illuminate the mind. One verse, older than anyone saying it. That's day one hundred eight.

109.title: Silent japa
109.howItsDone: Hindu practitioners do japa aloud, whispered or silently in the mind; many meditation lineages teach so-ham (hamsa) with the breath, describing the ajapa japa as the mantra the breath repeats on its own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri: the oldest mantra, asking the sun to light up our minds. Your line was light, illuminate the mind. Today, the mantra goes quiet.

You know how a song gets stuck in your head? You didn't decide to hum it. You're brushing your teeth and there it is, playing by itself. Annoying, when it's an advertising jingle. But what if it were something you'd chosen? The tradition noticed this long ago. Say a mantra out loud long enough, and one day you catch it going on inside you while you're doing something else entirely. Nobody's saying it. It's saying itself. There's a word for that.
screen: `A SONG STUCK IN YOUR HEAD.` → `WHAT IF YOU CHOSE THE SONG?` → `NOBODY IS SAYING IT.`

segments.voice: Japa comes three ways. Out loud, as you did with Hare Krishna, is vachika, spoken. Whispered, lips moving, barely a sound, is upamshu. Silent, only in the mind, is manasika, mental. Several old texts and teachers rank these, and they put the silent one highest: the quieter it gets, they say, the deeper it goes in. Not because out loud is wrong, but because silent japa has nowhere to hide. No sound to lean on, just you and the mantra. Then there's a fourth thing, which isn't really a way of doing japa at all: ajapa. The a at the front means not. Not-repeating: the mantra that happens without anyone doing it. The yoga traditions describe it with the breath. Some teachers say the in-breath makes a soft sound like so, and the out-breath a sound like ham. So-ham, a Sanskrit phrase meaning I am that. The old texts say every living being repeats it with every breath, all day and all night, thousands of times a day, without knowing. They call it the ajapa gayatri, the Gayatri that isn't said. You can't force ajapa; you can only notice it. So you start with silent japa, then gradually let go of saying it, and see if the breath carries it on. It says itself.
screen: `SPOKEN, WHISPERED, SILENT.` · `THE QUIETER, THE DEEPER.` · `AJAPA — NOT-REPEATING.` · `SO ON THE IN-BREATH, HAM ON THE OUT.` · then, large: `IT SAYS ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Settle into your breath and say your mantra silently, the one that fits or simply so-ham: so as you breathe in, ham as you breathe out, no lips, no whisper. After a while, stop saying it on purpose and just listen for the so and the ham in the breath. If you lose it, start saying it again, gently, and let go again.
Ajapa. Not-repeating. The mantra that goes on by itself, carried on the breath: so on the way in, ham on the way out.
Your line: it says itself. The breath has been saying it all along. Day one hundred nine.

110.title: A full round
110.howItsDone: Hindus doing japa commonly use a mala of 108 beads plus a larger meru bead, moving one bead per mantra with the thumb and middle finger, and turning back at the meru rather than crossing it; one full round is 108 repetitions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ajapa: the mantra that says itself, so on the in-breath, ham on the out. Your line was it says itself. Today, the end of mantra week, and your first full round.

Pick up a japa mala, a string of prayer beads, and count. Very often: one hundred and eight. Plus one more, bigger, set apart, often with a tassel. Gods have lists of 108 names, recited as one long litany of praise. Some sacred places are counted in sets of 108. The number keeps turning up. Ask people why, and you'll get plenty of confident answers, and they won't match.
screen: `108 BEADS, PLUS ONE.` → `108 NAMES, 108 PLACES.` → `MANY ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Nobody knows for certain why 108. Here are some answers people give, and you can enjoy them without picking one. It's one, times two squared, times three cubed: one times four times twenty-seven. People love that. There's a traditional list of 108 Upanishads. Tradition gives 108 names for Vishnu, for Shiva, for the Goddess, for Ganesha. Which of these came first, if any, nobody knows, and the texts don't say. What people do share is a sense that 108 makes a full round. Complete. Now, how a round works. The big bead is the meru, like the sacred mountain at the center of the world, also called the guru bead. You start next to it. Hold the mala in your right hand, draped over the middle finger, and pull each bead toward you with your thumb, one bead per mantra. Many teachers say to keep the index finger off the beads, pointing away; some explain it as the finger of ego, but not every lineage says so. When you come back around to the meru, you don't cross it. You stop. For another round, turn the mala around and go back the way you came. And that's the week. You found the one that fits, bowed to Shiva's stillness, asked Ganesha to clear the road, sang the name, held the Gayatri's light and let the mantra say itself. Now, one full round. Complete is enough. 108 is enough.
screen: `NOBODY KNOWS FOR CERTAIN WHY.` · `A FULL ROUND, COMPLETE.` · `THE MERU BEAD: DON'T CROSS IT.` · `THUMB PULLS, INDEX FINGER AWAY.` · then, large: `108 IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Pick your mantra, the one that fits, or Om, or Om Namah Shivaya, and begin beside the big bead, or on your finger joints, twelve per hand counted with the thumb, nine times through. One bead, one mantra, softly or silently; the bell will ring before you finish, and that's fine, so keep going until you reach the meru. Then don't start another; sit for three breaths.
Meru, the big bead you stop at, not cross: the guru bead ending the mala's 108, one full round, complete.
Your line: 108 is enough. One full round, complete, and then you rest. Mantra week, done.

111.title: Five objects
111.hook: a shelf in five things: image, lamp, flower, bell, water
111.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep a small shrine, from a whole puja room to a kitchen shelf, with an image or picture of the family's deities, a lamp, flowers, a bell and water, where daily puja is offered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the meru, and your first full round of 108 on the mala. Your line was 108 is enough. This week, the practice gets a home. Literally.

In many Hindu homes there's a small shrine. In a big house it might be a whole room. In a student apartment it's a shelf above the desk. In a lot of kitchens it's a little alcove near the stove, with a picture of Krishna leaning against the spice jars and a lamp lit every morning for as long as anyone remembers. It's called the mandir, the temple, or the puja room, even when it's only a shelf. Nobody needs permission to make one. And a simple one can come down to five things.
screen: `A ROOM, OR A SHELF.` → `KRISHNA BY THE SPICE JARS.` → `IT COMES DOWN TO FIVE THINGS.`

segments.voice: One: an image. A small statue, called a murti, or a picture: your ishta, the face you're drawn to, or Ganesha, or the family's deity. Many Hindus understand the image as a place where the divine is present, and treat it like an honored guest. Others see it as a focus for the mind. Both are held. Two: a lamp, small, clay or brass, with oil or ghee and a cotton wick. Light is offered, and tomorrow the lamp gets a whole day. Three: a flower, fresh if you can. Something beautiful, given away, that won't last. Four: a bell, a small hand bell rung at the start of puja, to call the attention of the divine, many say, and your own. Five: water, a small cup or pot of it, clean, offered, sipped, sprinkled. Nothing on that list is expensive. That's the point: the care counts, not the cost. Where does it go? Traditions offer guidance. Many prefer the image facing east or west, with you facing it, in a spot that's clean and a little apart, not in the bathroom or under the stairs. But a home shrine grows out of the life you actually have. A clean shelf you pass every morning is better than a perfect room you never enter. This week you'll build yours, piece by piece. Today, just the corner. A corner that's yours.
screen: `AN IMAGE — THE HONORED GUEST.` · `A LAMP, A FLOWER.` · `A BELL, AND WATER.` · `NOTHING HERE IS EXPENSIVE.` · then, large: `A CORNER THAT'S YOURS.`

segments.voice: Choose a place, a shelf, the corner of a dresser, a windowsill, and clear it, even if you only wipe it with your hand. Gather what you have: an image or a picture that means something to you, a candle or tea light, a flower or a leaf from outside, anything that rings, even a spoon on a glass, and a small cup of water, and set them down slowly. If you can't do it right now, picture exactly where it will go, then sit in front of it and breathe.
Five objects. An image, a lamp, a flower, a bell, and water: the whole home shrine, in five simple things.
Your line: a corner that's yours. A shelf is plenty. One hundred eleven days in.

112.title: The lamp
112.hook: lighting it, what the flame is
112.howItsDone: Many Hindu households light a small lamp, often a clay diya with a cotton wick in ghee or oil, at the home shrine at dawn and at dusk, and many say a short Sanskrit verse to the lamp's light as they do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five objects: an image, a lamp, a flower, a bell, a little water. Your line was a corner that's yours.

The power goes out at night. The fridge stops humming. Everyone goes quiet. Somebody fumbles in a drawer, finds a candle, strikes a match. And the whole room changes. Faces come back. People talk more softly, as if the little flame were listening. One small light, and a dark house becomes a place again. Many homes do that on purpose, every evening, even when the power is fine. It's the second object on the shelf, and the one many homes start with. Today: the lamp.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `ONE MATCH, AND THE ROOM CHANGES.` → `TODAY: THE LAMP.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is deepa, from a root that means to shine, to blaze. In a lot of homes it's a tiny clay bowl, a diya, with a twist of cotton for a wick, sitting in ghee or oil. Some families use brass, some a tea light. The flame is the point, not the holder. Many Hindu households light it twice a day, at dawn and at dusk, the edges of the day. Many families say a short Sanskrit verse as they light it, one that begins shubham karoti kalyanam: it honors the lamp's light as bringing what is good, health and plenty, and pushing away what harms. Here's what people say the flame is. First, a way of saying the divine is here: the lamp is often lit before anything else is offered. Second, a prayer for what lasts. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad has an often-recited line asking to be led from darkness to light, and it explains itself: darkness there is death, and light is what does not die. Many teachers also hear darkness as not knowing. The lamp is that line with a match. And people point out two small things that make a flame a teacher. However you tilt the lamp, the flame still points up. And when one lamp lights another, it loses nothing. You can light a hundred wicks from one, and the first burns just as bright. That's why, back on day five, arti was light passed hand to hand. It all starts with one.

segments.voice: If it's safe, light a candle or a lamp somewhere steady, away from anything that can catch; if not, picture one. Let your eyes rest on the flame softly, without staring hard, and notice how it moves with your breath, the bright middle, the blue at the base. Then close your eyes for a moment, see if the shape of it stays, and open them: one flame, that's all.
Deepa. The lamp: a small flame, from a root meaning to shine, lit at the edges of the day.
Your line: one flame. A light passed on to another loses nothing at all. Until tomorrow.
